scenario_stem:
Alderbrace Construction Ltd is a private limited company building 30 family homes a year on the edge of Dunmore, a growing town in Country X. The business owns 2 tower cranes, 14 lorries and 6 excavators, and employs 58 site workers plus 7 office staff. Land for a third housing phase was bought for $2.1m last year.

Managing director Priya Nair is deciding whether to buy a new $380,000 mobile crane or to hire 12 additional bricklayers at $520 a week each for the next 3 years. Each bricklayer could lay 340 bricks a day, while the crane would lift loads 4 times faster than the existing hoist. Last year site output rose 11% after new machinery was installed, yet 22 houses from the latest phase remain unsold.

questions.question_text: Define 'capital' as a factor of production.
questions.model_answer: Capital is the man-made resources used to produce goods and services, such as Alderbrace's 2 tower cranes, 14 lorries, 6 excavators and hoist, which are used to build homes. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Capital = man-made / human-made resources used to produce goods and services
Reward any suitable examples such as machinery, tools, vehicles, equipment or buildings

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why capital is important to Alderbrace Construction Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Capital gives a business the man-made resources it needs to produce goods and services [k]. Alderbrace owns 2 tower cranes, 14 lorries and 6 excavators to build its 30 family homes a year [app]. Reason 2: Capital raises productivity because machines can work faster and longer than people alone [k]. After new machinery was installed last year, site output rose 11%, showing capital equipment measurably increased production [app].

knowledge_max_2: Capital = man-made resources used in production (machinery, vehicles, tools)
Capital goods help raise output and productivity
application_max_2: Alderbrace's own assets: 2 tower cranes, 14 lorries, 6 excavators / 30 family homes a year
The 11% rise in site output after new machinery was installed

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of buying the $380,000 mobile crane for Alderbrace.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Capital equipment can increase the speed of production [k]. The crane would lift loads 4 times faster than the existing hoist, allowing the firm to complete phases more quickly [app]. Faster lifting would reduce the time each house spends under construction, raising overall output and helping clear unsold stock sooner [an]. Benefit 2: Machinery raises efficiency by getting more output from existing inputs [k]. A $380,000 crane costs far less over 3 years than hiring 12 bricklayers at $520 a week, which would total $973,440 (12 x $520 x 156 weeks) [app]. Paying once for the crane instead of ongoing wages would cut production costs per house and improve profit margins [an].

knowledge_max_2: Machinery/capital equipment can increase speed and output
Machinery can reduce average costs / raise efficiency versus ongoing wages
application_max_2: Crane lifts loads 4 times faster than the existing hoist
Cost comparison: $380,000 crane versus $973,440 to hire 12 bricklayers over 3 years
analysis_max_2: Faster lifting shortens build time, raising output and sales turnover
Lower labour cost per house improves profit margins on the remaining houses

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderbrace Construction Ltd should buy the $380,000 mobile crane rather than hire 12 additional bricklayers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the crane: buying the $380,000 mobile crane gives Alderbrace more capital, which is a man-made resource for production [k]. It would lift loads 4 times faster than the existing hoist, and site output already rose 11% after the previous machinery was installed [app]. This suggests further capital investment would raise productivity and shorten build times, helping shift the 22 houses that remain unsold [an]. Argument for hiring bricklayers: hiring 12 bricklayers at $520 a week is more flexible and avoids a large one-off outlay [k]. However, 12 bricklayers over the next 3 years would cost $973,440 (12 x $520 x 156 weeks), far more than the crane's one-off $380,000 [app]. Yet with 22 houses still unsold, committing cash to the crane is risky if demand weakens, because a specialised crane cannot easily be resold or redeployed [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures the crane is cheaper over 3 years ($380,000 versus $973,440) and matches the 11% output gain from the earlier machinery, so Alderbrace should buy the crane if it can secure buyer interest in the remaining houses [eval]. If demand stays weak, flexible bricklayers would protect the firm's cash, so the decision depends on confirmed sales [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Crane = capital investment; bricklayers = labour, both are factors of production
Capital can raise productivity and reduce unit costs over time
application_max_2: $380,000 crane versus 12 x $520 x 156 weeks = $973,440 over 3 years
4 times faster lifting / 11% output rise / 22 houses remain unsold / $2.1m land purchase
analysis_max_2: Cost comparison over 3 years favours the crane if demand holds
Fixed capital carries resale/redeployment risk versus flexible labour given unsold stock
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation conditional on confirmed demand/buyer contracts for the remaining houses
Balanced judgement recognising flexibility of labour against the crane's cost saving

scenario_stem:
Vantara Logistics Ltd is a third-party fulfilment business operating a 9,000 sq m warehouse in the port city of Hallwick, Country X. It employs 340 warehouse operatives and processes 1,150 customer orders a day for 40 retail clients. Work on the packing line is split between 5 stations: receiving, picking, packing, labelling and dispatch.

Each operative is assigned to a single station and repeats the same task throughout the shift. Since the line was split into stations 18 months ago, output per worker per hour has risen from 62 to 74 orders. General manager Laura Chen is deciding whether to add a 6th station for quality checks or to train staff to rotate between all 5 stations. Wages currently average $11 per hour.

questions.question_text: Define 'division of labour'.
questions.model_answer: Division of labour is the splitting of the production process into separate tasks, with each worker specialising in one task, such as Vantara's operatives working at the receiving, picking, packing, labelling or dispatch stations. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Division of labour = production process broken down into separate tasks/operations
Workers specialise in a single task (allow examples such as the 5 stations)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why division of labour increases output at Vantara's warehouse.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Division of labour lets workers specialise in one task, so they become skilled and faster at it [k]. Since work was split into 5 stations, output per worker per hour has risen from 62 to 74 orders [app]. Reason 2: Specialisation reduces time lost switching between different tasks [k]. With 340 operatives each repeating the same task every shift, the line processes 1,150 orders a day without workers pausing to change roles [app].

knowledge_max_2: Specialising in one task raises skill, speed and dexterity
No time is lost switching between tasks
application_max_2: Output per worker per hour rose from 62 to 74 after stations were introduced
340 operatives / 1,150 orders a day / 5 named stations

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks of division of labour for Vantara.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: Doing the same task all shift can become boring and demotivating [k]. Operatives repeat the same task throughout the shift at $11 per hour, which could lower morale and increase absence [app]. Low motivation may push error rates up and force Vantara to spend more on supervision, reducing the gains from its split line [an]. Drawback 2: The line depends on every station working [k]. If the picking station stops, the operatives at packing, labelling and dispatch also run short of work, as the 5 stations are linked in sequence [app]. One absence or breakdown could therefore cut output across the whole warehouse, not just one step [an].

knowledge_max_2: Repetitive work causes boredom / low morale / reduced motivation
Interdependent tasks mean one stoppage halts the whole line
application_max_2: $11 per hour wages and repetitive single-task shifts
5 linked stations; picking feeds packing and labelling
analysis_max_2: Boredom can raise errors and absenteeism, eroding efficiency gains
Linked stations mean a single stoppage reduces total daily output of 1,150 orders

questions.question_text: Do you think Vantara should add a 6th quality-check station rather than train staff to rotate between all 5 stations? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the 6th station: adding a dedicated quality-check station would extend division of labour, a method that already raised output from 62 to 74 orders per worker per hour [k]. It would catch picking and packing errors before dispatch, protecting the service given to 40 retail clients [app]. This should raise accuracy without disrupting the current specialisation that delivers 1,150 orders a day [an]. Argument for rotation: training staff to rotate between all 5 stations would make work more varied and less boring [k]. It would also let Vantara cover absences and peak periods without hiring, protecting client service while wages average $11 per hour [app]. However, rotating staff could reduce the task-specific skill that lifted output by 12 orders per worker per hour over 18 months [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, adding the 6th station builds on proven gains of 62 to 74 orders per hour and protects quality for 40 clients, so Vantara should add the quality-check station and offer limited job rotation to the most experienced operatives [eval]. If errors are rare and morale is the bigger problem, rotation would be better, so the final decision should depend on error-rate data [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Quality checks / an extra station extend division of labour
Rotation makes work more varied and flexible but may dilute specialisation
application_max_2: 62 to 74 orders per worker per hour; 1,150 orders a day; 40 retail clients
$11 wages; 18 months since stations were introduced; 5 stations
analysis_max_2: 6th station catches errors before dispatch, protecting client reputation
Rotation risks losing the task-specific productivity gains built up over 18 months
evaluation_max_2: Recommends the 6th station, with rotation reserved for experienced operatives
Conditional judgement based on error-rate data versus staff morale

scenario_stem:
Brackmoor Haulage Co is a road freight company based in the market town of Fenwick, Country X, founded 11 years ago by brothers Tom and Nick Brady. It operates 28 HGVs serving the northern industrial corridor, and its 34 drivers each specialise on one of 3 fixed routes. Drivers receive 2 weeks of route-specific training before their first trip.

The company carries 1,900 tonnes of goods a month, and fuel use per kilometre has fallen 14% since drivers were assigned fixed routes. Managing director Tom Brady is considering whether to keep the 3 fixed routes or switch to flexible scheduling, in which drivers cover any route as needed. Two national supermarket contracts require deliveries within 90 minutes of scheduled times, with penalties of $1,200 per late load.

questions.question_text: Define 'specialisation'.
questions.model_answer: Specialisation is when a worker, business or region focuses on one product or one task, such as Brackmoor's drivers each specialising on one of the 3 fixed routes. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Specialisation = concentrating on one product, service or task
Workers or firms focus on what they do best (allow fixed-route driver examples)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why specialisation benefits Brackmoor Haulage Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Specialisation lets drivers become expert on particular routes, saving time and fuel [k]. Since drivers were assigned fixed routes, fuel use per kilometre has fallen 14%, and the company carries 1,900 tonnes a month [app]. Reason 2: Specialisation builds experience and knowledge that reduce mistakes [k]. Drivers receive 2 weeks of route-specific training before their first trip, and the 3 fixed routes help supermarket contracts arrive within the 90-minute window [app].

knowledge_max_2: Specialists become expert, faster and make fewer mistakes
Experience reduces waste of fuel, time and money
application_max_2: Fuel use per kilometre fell 14% after fixed routes were assigned
1,900 tonnes a month; 2 weeks route-specific training; 90-minute delivery windows; 3 fixed routes

questions.question_text: Explain two risks of specialisation for Brackmoor.
questions.model_answer: Risk 1: Relying on a few drivers per route creates dependency if a specialist is absent [k]. With only 34 drivers covering 3 fixed routes, illness or resignation could leave a route uncovered [app]. A missed supermarket delivery would cost $1,200 in penalties per late load, directly hitting profit [an]. Risk 2: Specialisation reduces flexibility when demand changes [k]. If one route's volume falls while another rises, fixed assignments could leave Brackmoor with unused capacity on one route and overtime on another [app]. Rigid schedules may make it harder to win new contracts outside the northern industrial corridor, limiting growth [an].

knowledge_max_2: Dependency on specialist staff / capacity lost if they are absent
Inflexibility when demand patterns change
application_max_2: 34 drivers across 3 fixed routes; 2 national supermarket contracts with 90-minute windows
$1,200 penalty per late load
analysis_max_2: A single absence can trigger $1,200 penalties and damage supermarket relationships
Rigid routes limit the ability to respond to demand changes or win work outside the corridor

questions.question_text: Do you think Brackmoor should keep its 3 fixed routes rather than switch to flexible scheduling? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for keeping fixed routes: specialisation has cut fuel use per kilometre by 14% since drivers were assigned fixed routes [k]. Fixed routes also support the 90-minute delivery windows in the 2 national supermarket contracts, where each late load costs $1,200 [app]. Dropping fixed routes would risk late deliveries, penalties and losing these contracts [an]. Argument for flexible scheduling: flexible cover would help if a specialist driver is ill and would let Brackmoor respond when volumes change between the 3 fixed routes [k]. It could also let the firm take on work outside the northern industrial corridor, using its 28 HGVs more fully [app]. However, flexible drivers would need retraining and fuel savings would likely fall below the 14% already achieved [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, keeping the 3 fixed routes is the safer choice because the 14% fuel saving and the $1,200-per-load penalties tied to 90-minute windows outweigh the flexibility benefit while the supermarket contracts run [eval]. If a key driver resigns or a major client leaves, Brackmoor should review the decision and consider partial flexibility [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Fixed routes underpin specialisation gains such as fuel savings
Flexible scheduling improves staff cover and adaptability
application_max_2: 14% fuel saving; 90-minute windows; $1,200 penalties; 2 national supermarket contracts
28 HGVs; 34 drivers; 3 fixed routes
analysis_max_2: Losing the fuel saving and risking penalties would damage profit and contracts
Flexibility has value for cover and new markets but dilutes driver expertise
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation favouring fixed routes while contracts run
Balanced judgement recognising partial flexibility if circumstances change

scenario_stem:
Solmere Warehousing Ltd runs a 12,000 sq m distribution warehouse in the town of Merriton, Country X, employing 96 staff and storing goods for 55 clients. Director Ade Johnson is deciding how to use a 5-hectare plot of land beside the warehouse. She could either expand the warehouse by 4,000 sq m at a cost of $1.6m to take on 25 new clients, or build a fleet yard and workshop to service 30 lorries.

The fleet yard, expected to save $210,000 a year in maintenance charges, would take 14 months to build, the same as the warehouse expansion. Solmere's annual profit is $780,000 and warehouse occupancy is 91%. Ade feels pressure from clients wanting more space, yet two of the fleet's lorries broke down last month, causing 9 missed deliveries.

questions.question_text: Define 'opportunity cost'.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made, such as the profits forgone from the fleet yard if Solmere spends the $1.6m on the warehouse expansion instead. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Opportunity cost = next best alternative forgone when a decision is made
Allow examples from the stem (fleet yard versus warehouse expansion)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why opportunity cost is important to Solmere's decision.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Opportunity cost measures what must be sacrificed when resources are limited [k]. Solmere has a 5-hectare plot that can serve only one of the two projects, the $1.6m expansion or the fleet yard [app]. Reason 2: Comparing opportunity costs helps the business choose the option with the greatest benefit [k]. The warehouse could take on 25 new clients with occupancy already at 91%, while the fleet yard would save $210,000 a year in maintenance charges [app].

knowledge_max_2: Opportunity cost = next best alternative forgone
Scarcity means choosing one option excludes the other
application_max_2: Single 5-hectare plot; only one project possible
$1.6m expansion for 25 new clients versus $210,000 annual maintenance saving; occupancy of 91%

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of the warehouse expansion for Solmere.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Adding 4,000 sq m of capacity would let Solmere serve more clients and raise revenue [k]. Occupancy is already 91% and the expansion would take on 25 new clients, each of whom would pay to store goods [app]. More clients would spread fixed costs over more pallet spaces, raising profit above the current $780,000 a year [an]. Advantage 2: Extra space reduces dependency on a single income stream [k]. Clients are already demanding more space, so expansion meets proven demand rather than speculative need [app]. Capturing that demand now would strengthen client loyalty and protect long-term revenue before rivals expand [an].

knowledge_max_2: Extra capacity allows more clients and higher revenue
Meeting existing demand builds loyalty and protects revenue
application_max_2: 91% occupancy; 25 new clients
$780,000 current profit; 55 existing clients
analysis_max_2: Higher occupancy spreads fixed costs and lifts profit above $780,000
Meeting proven demand defends market share and long-term revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Solmere should expand the warehouse by 4,000 sq m rather than build the fleet yard and workshop? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the expansion: a 4,000 sq m expansion costing $1.6m would directly meet client demand, with occupancy already at 91% and 55 clients asking for more space [k]. It would let Solmere take on 25 new clients, pushing annual profit above the current $780,000 [app]. The expansion builds Solmere's core storage business, where skills and occupancy already exist [an]. Argument for the fleet yard: building the yard and workshop would service 30 lorries and save $210,000 a year in maintenance charges, and it would address the 9 missed deliveries caused by 2 lorry breakdowns [k]. A reliable fleet could protect logistics contracts without the risk of half-empty warehouse space [app]. However, the $210,000 yearly saving is modest against a $1.6m capital outlay, and the yard does nothing to ease client pressure for space [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, the warehouse expansion is the better use of the 5-hectare plot because 91% occupancy and proven client demand make new profit more likely than the yard's $210,000 annual saving [eval]. Solmere should, however, repair the 2 failing lorries immediately whatever it decides [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Expansion meets existing client demand and raises capacity
Fleet yard saves maintenance costs and improves reliability
application_max_2: 91% occupancy; 25 new clients; $780,000 profit; $1.6m expansion cost
$210,000 yearly saving; 30 lorries; 2 breakdowns; 9 missed deliveries
analysis_max_2: Expansion revenue is likely to exceed yard savings given 91% occupancy and waiting demand
Yard's $210,000 yearly saving is modest relative to $1.6m capital and ignores the space shortage
evaluation_max_2: Recommends the expansion based on occupancy and proven demand
Balanced judgement acknowledging both options, with urgent lorry repairs regardless

scenario_stem:
Garnet Fleet Services is a fleet management company in the city of Corvane, Country X. It manages 210 vehicles for 68 client businesses, handling maintenance, insurance and compliance. Most clients are local hauliers and delivery companies. The firm employs 21 coordinators who each look after an average of 10 vehicles. Fleet management fees average $310 per vehicle a month.

Vehicle tracking software costing $95,000 was introduced in January and average jobs completed per vehicle per day have since risen from 9.4 to 11.2, a 19% increase. However, fuel costs have climbed 7% over the same period. Director Megan Osei is deciding whether to invest a further $130,000 in route-optimisation software or to offer her coordinators a 6% pay rise, as two senior coordinators have been approached by rival firms.

questions.question_text: Define 'productivity'.
questions.model_answer: Productivity measures how much output is produced per unit of input, such as jobs completed per vehicle per day, which rose from 9.4 to 11.2 at Garnet after tracking software was introduced. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Productivity = output per input / output per worker, machine or hour
Reward examples such as jobs per vehicle per day

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why productivity matters to Garnet Fleet Services.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Higher productivity means more output from the same resources, raising revenue [k]. Jobs per vehicle per day have risen from 9.4 to 11.2, a 19% increase since January [app]. Reason 2: Higher productivity spreads fixed costs over more jobs, improving efficiency [k]. With 21 coordinators each managing 10 vehicles, higher jobs per vehicle means more completed per coordinator without extra headcount [app].

knowledge_max_2: Productivity = output per unit of input
Higher productivity raises revenue and lowers unit costs
application_max_2: Jobs per vehicle per day rose from 9.4 to 11.2 (19% increase)
21 coordinators; 10 vehicles each; 210 vehicles; 68 client businesses

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of increasing productivity for Garnet.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Productivity gains let Garnet earn more from its existing fleet [k]. 210 vehicles complete 19% more jobs per day after tracking was introduced, so revenue per vehicle rose without buying new vehicles [app]. Extra jobs without extra capital directly raise profit per vehicle and help please the 68 client businesses [an]. Benefit 2: Productivity data supports better pricing and planning [k]. Knowing each vehicle now completes 11.2 jobs a day lets Garnet set accurate schedules and fees for its $310-per-vehicle monthly management service [app]. Reliable data helps Garnet keep clients and justify its fees against rival fleet managers [an].

knowledge_max_2: More output from the same resources raises profit
Accurate data supports planning, pricing and retention
application_max_2: Jobs per vehicle per day 11.2 (from 9.4); 19% increase
210 vehicles; 68 client businesses; $310 per vehicle per month
analysis_max_2: Extra jobs without new capital directly raise profit per vehicle
Accurate data supports pricing, client retention and competitiveness

questions.question_text: Do you think Garnet should invest $130,000 in route-optimisation software rather than offer a 6% pay rise? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for the software: route-optimisation builds on the productivity gain already achieved, with jobs per vehicle per day rising from 9.4 to 11.2, a 19% increase, after the $95,000 tracking investment [k]. Spending $130,000 more could raise productivity further and help cut fuel use, which has already climbed 7% [app]. The software directly targets efficiency and should raise profit per vehicle across the fleet [an]. Argument for the pay rise: a 6% pay rise would help keep the two senior coordinators who have been approached by rival firms, protecting their knowledge of the 10 vehicles each and the service given to 68 client businesses [k]. Losing senior staff would raise recruitment and training costs and could lower productivity more than software would lift it [app]. However, a pay rise raises fixed costs permanently, while software is a one-off cost with lasting efficiency benefits [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Garnet should invest in the $130,000 route-optimisation software because the 19% productivity gain shows technology works, but it should first renegotiate with the two senior coordinators so the roll-out is not undermined [eval]. If both coordinators resign despite talks, the pay rise would matter more, so securing them is the urgent first step [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Pay rise retains key staff; software raises productivity
Technology cost versus labour cost trade-off
application_max_2: $130,000 software; 9.4 to 11.2 jobs per vehicle per day (19%); 7% fuel increase
6% pay rise; two senior coordinators; 68 client businesses; 10 vehicles each
analysis_max_2: Software leverages the proven 19% gain and addresses the 7% fuel-cost rise
Pay rise avoids recruitment and training costs but raises permanent fixed costs
evaluation_max_2: Recommends software, conditional on retaining the two senior coordinators
Balanced judgement of permanent wage cost versus one-off technology investment

scenario_stem:
Brindle Wharf Logistics operates a distribution warehouse beside the port of Alderquay, Country X, storing imported goods for 38 clients. It owns 46 fork-lift trucks and 12 reach trucks, keeping 150 staff busy across 3 shifts. The warehouse covers 11,000 sq m. Its busiest month is December, with 2,400 pallet movements a week. Last year the fleet broke down 27 times, costing $3,800 a month in lost time and repairs.

Director Carl Whitmore is weighing whether to build an in-house maintenance workshop costing $85,000 a year, including two full-time mechanics paid $16 an hour, or to sign an external service contract at $2,900 a month with a guaranteed 48-hour response. He believes Brindle must cut waste and run its resources more efficiently to protect its 9% operating margin.

questions.question_text: Define 'efficiency'.
questions.model_answer: Efficiency means producing the maximum output from given inputs with minimum waste, such as Brindle getting the most deliveries from its 46 fork-lift trucks and 12 reach trucks with the least wasted time and money. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Efficiency = maximum output from inputs / minimum waste
Best use of resources to achieve output (accept efficiency defined in contrast to productivity if accurate)

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why efficiency matters to Brindle Wharf Logistics.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Efficient operations lower costs and protect profit [k]. The fleet broke down 27 times last year, costing $3,800 a month in lost time and repairs [app]. Reason 2: Efficient use of equipment keeps goods moving on time for clients [k]. Brindle stores imported goods for 38 clients with 150 staff across 3 shifts, so wasted time directly delays dispatches [app].

knowledge_max_2: Efficiency lowers costs and waste, protecting profit
Efficient processes keep customer service reliable
application_max_2: 27 breakdowns; $3,800 a month in losses
38 clients; 150 staff; 3 shifts; December peak of 2,400 pallet movements a week

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Brindle could improve its efficiency.
questions.model_answer: Way 1: Regular preventive maintenance would reduce breakdowns [k]. The fleet broke down 27 times last year, and either an in-house workshop at $85,000 a year or an external contract at $2,900 a month would service trucks before they fail [app]. Fewer breakdowns would cut the $3,800 monthly losses and reduce idle staff time [an]. Way 2: Better shift planning would cut wasted waiting time [k]. With 150 staff across 3 shifts and goods for 38 clients, matching staffing to weekly pallet movements would reduce overtime and bottlenecks [app]. Smoother flow would raise throughput per worker and protect the 9% operating margin [an].

knowledge_max_2: Preventive maintenance reduces breakdowns
Better planning/scheduling cuts waste of time and labour
application_max_2: 27 breakdowns; $3,800 a month; options of $85,000 a year or $2,900 a month
150 staff; 3 shifts; 38 clients; 9% operating margin
analysis_max_2: Fewer breakdowns cut losses and idle time, raising efficiency
Matching staffing to demand raises throughput and protects the operating margin

questions.question_text: Do you think Brindle should build the in-house maintenance workshop rather than sign the external service contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Argument for in-house: an in-house workshop lets Brindle service trucks immediately, cutting the 27 breakdowns that cost $3,800 a month in lost time and repairs [k]. Including two mechanics paid $16 an hour, it costs $85,000 a year but keeps expertise on site for 46 fork-lift trucks and 12 reach trucks [app]. Faster repairs mean less downtime, higher throughput and more reliable service, protecting the 9% operating margin [an]. Argument for external: the $2,900 monthly contract costs $34,800 a year (12 x $2,900), less than half the in-house cost [k]. The guaranteed 48-hour response covers emergencies without paying two mechanics' fixed wages, though 48-hour delays could still disrupt dispatch for its 38 clients [app]. Slower response risks more lost pallet movements and strained client trust than the saving justifies [an]. Overall, on the stem's figures, Brindle should sign the external contract first because $34,800 a year is far cheaper than $85,000, which matters on a 9% operating margin, while it measures whether response times protect client service [eval]. If breakdowns persist or response times slip, the in-house workshop would become the better choice [eval].

knowledge_max_2: In-house = fast, dedicated maintenance capability
External = cheaper outsourced service, slower response
application_max_2: $85,000 in-house including two mechanics at $16 an hour; $2,900 a month = $34,800 a year
27 breakdowns; $3,800 monthly losses; 46 fork-lift trucks; 12 reach trucks; 38 clients
analysis_max_2: Faster repairs reduce downtime and protect client service and the 9% margin
External contract saves money but 48-hour delay risks disruption and client trust
evaluation_max_2: Recommends the external contract with conditions, reviewing if breakdowns persist
Recognises margin pressure versus service-quality trade-off between the two options

scenario_stem:
Ferromere Construction Co is a civil engineering contractor in Country X that has grown from 12 to 140 staff in 9 years. It specialises in rail and road infrastructure across the northern provinces. Founder and managing director Elena Petrova has spotted a chance to bid for a 3-year, $8.6m government contract to build a rail depot.

Elena must choose between this $8.6m depot bid and continuing with small housing refurbishments, which earn $95,000 profit per project with an 85% success rate. The depot would require hiring 60 workers within 6 months and a performance bond of 5% of the contract value. Last year Ferromere earned $1.3m profit on $9.5m revenue. Housing refurbishments make up 70% of the firm's income. A decision is needed by the end of the quarter.

questions.question_text: Define 'enterprise'.
questions.model_answer: Enterprise is the factor of production that organises land, labour and capital and takes risks to run a business and spot opportunities, such as Elena Petrova founding Ferromere and bidding for contracts. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Enterprise = organising the other factors of production
Risk-taking and decision-making by entrepreneurs to start/run a business

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why enterprise is important to Ferromere Construction Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Enterprise organises land, labour and capital into productive activity [k]. Elena has grown Ferromere from 12 to 140 staff in 9 years by coordinating teams across northern rail and road projects [app]. Reason 2: Enterprise spots and seizes business opportunities [k]. Elena is bidding for a 3-year, $8.6m government rail depot contract, showing she identifies profitable chances for the firm [app].

knowledge_max_2: Enterprise organises the other factors (land, labour, capital)
Entrepreneurs take risks, spot opportunities and make decisions
application_max_2: Grew from 12 to 140 staff in 9 years
$8.6m, 3-year rail depot contract bid; northern provinces

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ferromere of winning the $8.6m depot contract.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Winning the contract would give Ferromere a large, secure revenue stream [k]. A 3-year, $8.6m project would add about $2.87m of revenue a year, more than twice the $1.3m profit Ferromere earned last year in annual terms [app]. Secure long-term work would smooth cash flow and support hiring 60 workers without idle capacity [an]. Benefit 2: Completing a high-profile government project would raise Ferromere's reputation [k]. scenario_stem:
Northchill Cold Chain Ltd runs temperature-controlled storage from 3 warehouses in the port city of Kellby, Country X. It stores frozen fish, meat and dairy products for 72 food clients, with a combined capacity of 6,800 pallet spaces. Each warehouse runs 24 hours a day and employs 28 staff. Demand for chilled space has grown 25% in 2 years, yet scarcity of suitable land limits expansion.

Warehouse manager Ruth Adeyemi is deciding how to use 400 spare pallet spaces at the Kellby No. 2 warehouse. She could sublet them to a new frozen-food exporter at $18 per pallet per month, earning $86,400 a year, or reserve them for existing clients who expect orders to expand 30% next year. Ruth must balance limited capacity against growing client demands.

It has only 400 spare pallet spaces at Kellby No. 2, while demand has grown 25% in 2 years [app]. Reason 2: Scarcity means an opportunity cost arises whichever option is picked [k]. Reserving the spaces for existing clients excludes the income from subletting to the new exporter at $18 per pallet per month [app].

This would increase revenue per pallet and send scarce space to the clients who value it most [an]. Way 2: Northchill could invest in expansion, such as a 4th warehouse, if suitable land and capital allow [k]. Suitable land is scarce and expensive, so expansion would take planning and money [app]. Extra pallet spaces would remove the bottleneck, increasing capacity so existing clients' growth can be served without subletting to exporters [an].
